label: first input token is u, d, or 0 (plus weaker step-3 echo)
explanation: Fires on essentially every sequence whose first input (t=0) is u, d or the digit 0 (precision 1.0 on dev); this is 77% of activation mass, with typical activation about 0.12-0.22 of max. A secondary component (about 20% of mass) fires at t=3 when the input is again u/d/0 (occasionally f/h) and the earlier prefix contains tokens like k, y, t, 1, n, s; this component carries the very largest activations (top examples are all k/y-initial sequences with u/d/0 at step 3) but is sparse and only partially predictable (adding it as first_tok in {k,y} raises F1 only 0.873 -> 0.877). Never fires at t=1, t>=5, or anywhere in the copy phase; a few weak activations at the delimiter. Does not fire on other letters at t=0, nor on u/d/0 at later positions in general.

issues: Label calls the step-3 component a 'weaker' echo. It is rarer (about 20% of mass), but it holds the largest activations (up to 0.61 of max in test misses), and top-quartile coverage of the predicate is only 0.71. The explanation text says this correctly; the label wording is misleading.

The t=3 component is only weakly predictable. (t==3)&in u/d/0 alone has precision 0.17. Prefix conditions (seen/n_seen of k,y,t,1,n,s; first_tok; no earlier u/d/0 or vowels) reach at most about 0.3-0.6 precision at low recall. So about 20% of mass stays unexplained, as the author acknowledged.

All factual claims verified. Test: P=1.0, R=0.774, F1=0.873, mass recall 0.763. Zero false positives. No activity at t=1, t>=5 or in the copy phase. Delimiter: 212 steps, 1.4% of mass. t=2 u/d/0: precision 0.03. f/h at t=3: precision 0.06.
Best extended predicate I found matches the author's alternative: test F1 0.887, mass recall 0.84. It is a modest gain, not a systematic gap.
